If you haven't slept enough, should you still exercise?

It depends.

If you're severely sleep deprived, dial back the intensity and prioritize recovery. However, the occasional bad night doesn't automatically mean you should skip exercise. In fact, exercise helps with part of the metabolic disruption that follows acute sleep deprivation.

Observationally, short sleep (less than 6 hours/night) is associated with higher mortality in people falling short of physical activity guidelines, but among those meeting the guidelines, that excess risk is absent or diminished.

I'm not saying that exercise cancels out insufficient sleep. But the data suggest staying active may buffer some of its consequences.

From my last appearance on @hubermanlab.
hits.draft_en:

It doesn't cancel out bad sleep. But it helps. Go lighter, but still go.

Paul Perkins stood in a hospital room over Thanksgiving weekend in 2019, staring at a stage 4 liver cancer diagnosis and the quiet calculation that he might have about 90 days left. 
He was 70. A former New York Times advertising executive, husband, father of three, Navy veteran. Not particularly active. Years of client entertainment had left their mark. The biopsy at NYU Langone brought better news—the cancer was slow-growing—but the message was clear: improve your physical health, change your diet, and exercise more, or the odds don’t improve. 
Perkins’ answer was immediate: “You don’t have to tell me twice. I’m going to be the most physically fit patient you’ve ever seen in your entire life.”
He started with 30-minute walks. Then he ran. Then he lifted. He watched hours of YouTube tutorials on core work and push-pull-legs routines. He virtually quit drinking and cleaned up how he ate. During COVID, he and his wife Juliana turned one bay of their three-car garage into a fully equipped home gym—cars parked outside so the barbells could stay inside. He logged sub-nine-minute miles and eventually bench-pressed his own bodyweight. 
The work was unglamorous and daily. An hour of warm-ups and dynamic stretching first, because, as he later put it, warming up becomes non-negotiable as you age. Interval running. Then the weights. Small, consistent meals. Sleep. Relationships. No magic pills. Just the boring, repeated decision to move even on the days he didn’t feel like it—the same way you brush your teeth. 
Five years later, after continued progress and a minor skin cancer scare, the relative novice entered the American Drug-Free Powerlifting Federation nationals in Boston. At 75 years old, standing 6 feet and about 165 pounds, he set tournament records in the squat and deadlift (best deadlift 105 kg / ~231 lb) and tied the bench mark in his age group. He won his weight class and was crowned the over-75 champion. The night before, Juliana had told him, “We didn’t drive five and a half hours for nothing. You better win.” Family, competitors, and spectators cheered. He still gets goosebumps thinking about the camaraderie. 
His kids took notice. Son Paris and daughter Tiffany now compete in bodybuilding; daughter Caroline started her own fitness program. Perkins’ simple message to anyone listening is the same one he gave himself: Just move. Start with walking or jumping jacks if that’s what you’ve got. Make it daily. Challenge yourself with new goals—he’s already eyeing Senior Games events that include powerlifting plus the pole vault, long jump, and high jump, building the core and jumping muscles while he keeps learning the technique. 
At 75 he is living proof that a serious diagnosis and a number on a birthday cake do not have to write the rest of the story. Consistency, movement, and the refusal to treat age as a finish line turned the patient who thought he had 90 days into a national champion.
Just move.

Breast cancer cells are LOADED with insulin receptors. That's important to know for preventing/treating it. Why? Read on...

In 159 breast tumors, insulin receptor content was more than 6 times higher than in normal breast tissue. And the receptors worked: they bound insulin and switched on.

Many cancer cells favor a form of the insulin receptor (IR-A) that acts mainly as a growth signal, not a sugar-handling one. Insulin tells these cells to grow.

So what happens when insulin runs high?

She has said that if you let whatever you’re dealing with control your life, you have no quality of life. At 85 she remains the only competitive powerlifter her age in the U.S. and is still getting after it.

In the spring of 1961, at Trenton State Hospital in New Jersey, a nurse pushed a needle into the arm of a 32-year-old mathematician and watched the clock.

John Nash—already famous for game theory, already slipping into the private universe of voices and conspiracies that would later make him the subject of A Beautiful Mind—had been transferred to the insulin unit. 

His Princeton colleagues had begged the hospital to put him there. It was better staffed than the regular wards. It was also the best treatment medicine had for schizophrenia.

Every morning, large doses of insulin drove his blood sugar so low that his brain shut down. He slipped into coma. His body stiffened. Sometimes he seized. Staff waited roughly an hour, then brought him back with a glucose solution, often through a tube. Day after day. Week after week. Six weeks in all.

Nash later called it torture. He remembered the surrounding rituals—the showers afterward, the sugar water, the group of other patients—but almost nothing of the coma itself. The treatment carved gaps in his memory. He resented it for years; on letters he sometimes listed his return address as “Insulin Institute.” During those weeks he also became a vegetarian, he later said, partly as a quiet protest against what he saw as cruelty.

The theory, developed by Austrian psychiatrist Manfred Sakel in the 1920s and 1930s, was that starving the brain of glucose would somehow jolt or “reset” psychotic thinking. Hospitals built special units. Patients were chosen carefully—those with recent onset and better odds. Reported success rates varied wildly; some doctors claimed dramatic recoveries, while critics noted that patients already likely to improve were selected and given intensive attention. Mortality ran roughly 1–5 percent. 

Permanent brain damage was a recognized risk. One contemporary study even suggested certain forms of brain damage were therapeutic because they reduced “tension and hostility.”

By the late 1950s the evidence was collapsing. A controlled trial found no difference between insulin comas and comas induced by barbiturates. Chlorpromazine and other antipsychotics proved safer and more practical. Within a decade the insulin units emptied.

Nash eventually stabilized enough to return to mathematics, though his recovery was long, uneven, and not simply a triumph of the treatment. He continued to struggle for years. Many others were not so fortunate. Singer-songwriter Townes Van Zandt, treated as a teenager in Galveston, lost large stretches of long-term memory; his mother later called allowing the therapy her biggest regret. 

Psychiatric survivor Leonard Roy Frank described dozens of forced insulin comas as “the most devastating, painful and humiliating experience of my life.”
Insulin coma therapy was not fringe quackery. For two decades it was mainstream, labor-intensive, and sincerely believed. It gave desperate doctors something concrete to do in an era when schizophrenia often meant lifelong institutionalization. 

It also left scars—literal and figurative—that patients carried long after the last insulin unit closed.

The mathematician’s mind eventually found its way back. The method that tried to force the journey never did.

In a quiet laboratory above the streets of Zagreb, Dr. Andrija Karačić stared at a set of bacterial profiles that refused to match the textbook.

Karačić, a Croatian physician who trained in abdominal surgery and later founded the country’s first dedicated Gut Microbiome Center (Centar za crijevni mikrobiom), had spent years studying how diet reshapes the trillions of microbes living in the human intestine. Like most of the field, he had absorbed the near-universal claim: remove plants and their fiber, and the microbiome collapses. Diversity plummets. Beneficial fiber-fermenting bacteria vanish. 

Pathological shifts follow. The carnivore diet—strictly animal foods, zero plants—should have been the perfect experiment to confirm that prediction.

In 2024 his team finally found a subject willing to be tested. The man was 32, healthy, physically active, and had eaten nothing but meat, eggs, butter, cream, and hard cheeses for four full years. No vegetables. No fruit. No grains. No legumes. He reported better skin, better digestion, and no health complaints. His bloodwork and body composition looked unremarkable for a lean, training man.

When the 16S sequencing results arrived from the partner lab in Germany, Karačić and his colleagues expected a barren landscape. What they saw instead was a microbiome dominated by Firmicutes and populated by genera classically labeled as fiber degraders: Faecalibacterium, Blautia, various Lachnospiraceae, Bacteroides, and Roseburia. Alpha and beta diversity matched carefully selected healthy omnivore controls of similar age, sex, and lifestyle. Predicted functional capacity was comparable. The carnivore’s profile was actually least similar to people who ate meat every day as part of a conventional mixed diet. 

The paper, titled “The gut microbiome without any plant food? A case study on the gut microbiome of a healthy carnivore,” became the first published long-term look at the topic. The authors were careful: one person is not a population, and elevated Escherichia and Salmonella sequences raised questions. Still, the central observation was hard to ignore. A man who had consumed essentially zero dietary fiber for years had not developed an obviously pathological, collapsed microbiome.

Karačić’s group kept looking. By 2026 they had assembled ten healthy adults who had stayed on a carnivore diet for an average of roughly three years (range extending beyond five). These were compared against 874 confounder-matched omnivore controls. Alpha-diversity was not reduced; the carnivores showed higher Chao1 richness, indicating more low-abundance taxa. There were no significant losses of Akkermansia muciniphila, the Lactobacillus group, or butyrate-related pathways. 

Taxonomic shifts appeared—enrichment of certain low-abundance phyla such as Synergistetes and Desulfobacterota, reductions in some Bifidobacterium and specific Faecalibacterium and Roseburia species—but multivariate models showed the diet itself, not age, BMI, sleep, or place of residence, was the dominant driver. 
Functional profiling told a more nuanced story. 

The carnivore microbiomes were enriched for amino-acid degradation, B-vitamin synthesis, energy metabolism, and protein fermentation. Some modules linked to cytotoxicity, inflammation, and constipation were also elevated. The authors noted potential long-term risks while emphasizing that the findings challenged the assumption that dietary fiber is required to maintain microbial diversity. They suggested certain animal-derived nutrients might exert previously under-appreciated prebiotic-like effects.

The work did not declare the carnivore diet universally safe or optimal. It did not claim the microbiome was identical to that of a fiber-rich eater. What it did was document, in healthy people living the diet for years rather than days, that the predicted pathological collapse had not occurred. The gut ecosystem had adapted

outsiders.name: Amjad Masad
outsiders.text:
For centuries, the architecture of the firm has barely changed: hierarchies of people organized into departments and coordinated through bureaucracy.

AI agents are about to upend that.

We’re moving toward the self-driving company where humans exercise judgment and agents execute most of the work.

At Replit, we’re building the foundation for this new kind of company. We’re calling it “the Agent Habitat.”

Marc Andreessen wrote a fantastic piece placing this shift in the history of computing. Every major computing revolution began with chaos before businesses figured out how to harness it.
